seo.title: Karmic tail 3 7 13 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 7 13 compatibility: The Empress, The Chariot and Death. Why a couple that outruns everything has to learn to change the shape of its union.

title: Karmic tail 3-7-13 in compatibility: a full house, a chariot and the Death no one can outrun
short: This couple's three cards trace a strange route: The Empress at the entry, a full house and growth; The Chariot in the middle, motion and victory; and Death as the main task. The answer to the riddle is that a union able to outrun any difficulty has to learn the one thing nobody outruns: how to end a form that has run its course and meet the partner again, as someone new.

sections.h2: The myth of Admetus and Alcestis: three cards in the order of the tail
paragraphs: Admetus is king of Pherae, a town in Thessaly. The opening of the story is told by the mythographers — the Library of Pseudo-Apollodorus (I, 9, 15) and the Fabulae of Hyginus (50 and 51). King Pelias promised his daughter Alcestis to whoever could yoke a lion and a boar to a chariot. Admetus was helped by Apollo, whom Zeus had sentenced to serve a mortal as a hired hand: the god yoked the beasts himself, and Admetus carried off his bride. At the wedding Admetus forgot to sacrifice to Artemis, and the bridal chamber was found full of snakes. Apollo smoothed that over too, and won from the Fates an unheard-of favour: when death came for Admetus, he could buy himself free if someone agreed to die in his place.

The day came. Admetus's old father and mother refused. His wife agreed. This is where Euripides' tragedy begins, staged in Athens in 438 BC. On the day Alcestis dies, Heracles calls at the house. The host hides his mourning from the guest so as not to break the law of hospitality. Heracles learns the truth, goes to the grave, wrestles Death and brings Admetus a veiled woman. It is Alcestis, but for three days she will not speak.

The three acts of the myth run exactly in the order of the cards. First a house where there is plenty of everything — **The Empress**. Then a chariot drawn by two animals that do not belong together — **The Chariot**. Then Death walks in at the door, and in Euripides this is no figure of speech: Thanatos is a character, arguing with Apollo outside the palace in the very first scene.

Euripides even fits the whole tail into a single stanza. The chorus sings the praises of Admetus's house: Apollo kept his flocks here, lions came down from the hills to his piping, the sheep are past counting, and the ploughland and pasture run out to the place "where the steeds of the sun halt, darkness-cumbered" (here and below in the translation by Arthur S. Way, 1894; line numbers follow the Greek text). Plenty, horses and darkness in one sentence: **the Empress's field ends where the sun unharnesses its chariot and night falls.**

One caveat straight away. In the myth Admetus is the husband and Alcestis the wife. In a couple, gender does not hand out the roles. Either partner can be the "Admetus" who outruns his own endings. Either can be the "Alcestis" who pays for the shared race with herself — her plans, her time, her voice. Often the two take turns.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Empress: a home with plenty of everything, for good
paragraphs: For Lisovskaya, the entry to the task is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a "common language". The same point also sits on the relationship line, so in these couples' reading The Empress appears twice: as "Entry to the task" and as "Common language". One and the same wish both joins the two and becomes the thing they run up against.

This couple's language is "more, and for good". They find it easy to agree on a bigger flat, a house in the country, a long table with room for friends and family, children, a business that keeps growing. Lisovskaya gives the key to the Empress as fertility, abundance and growth, and in the plus she describes comfort, care, shared projects and learning to handle money as a family. People like this are warm to be around, and it is not an act.

In Euripides, Admetus's house is a model of this entry. The chorus calls it "the home of the free", thronged with guests. Even on the day of the funeral Admetus will not turn Heracles away: "mine halls have not learnt to thrust away nor to dishonour guests" (566–567). Alcestis's last morning is about the house too. She bathed in river water, put on her finest clothes, stood at the hearth and prayed for her children: a loving wife for her son, a noble husband for her daughter. Then she went round every altar in the palace and wreathed it with myrtle. Then she said goodbye to the marriage bed and held out her right hand to every servant: "none there was so mean to whom she spake not and received reply". Before she dies she asks for one thing: keep the house for the children and do not bring in a stepmother.

The clue is in the vocabulary. In Waite's list of divinatory meanings, The Empress has "Fruitfulness, action, initiative, length of days". In Edward Coleridge's English translation, these are the very words Admetus throws at his father: "I see thy heart is set on length of days" (715). His father accuses him of the same thing: "Cunning device hast thou devised to die never, cajoling still wife after wife to die for thee!" (699–701). Both of them want a long life. **In the minus, the wish at the entry sounds like this: let it all be ours, and let nothing ever end.**

This is where plus turns into minus. Among the tasks of a couple with The Empress, Lisovskaya names getting out from under the influence of the mother and the wider family, and growing out of childishness. Admetus expected his parents to pay for his long life — literally, with theirs. In an ordinary couple it is quieter: the plan for the big home rests on the parents' money, on somebody's unpaid work, on one of the two agreeing to "wait for now". When the parents say no, the couple takes offence, like Admetus: "For in word only, not in deed, they loved me" (339).

sections.h2: Middle of the task — The Chariot: a lion and a boar in one harness
paragraphs: Lisovskaya gives the middle of the tail no meaning of its own; it is an "addition" to the main task. In our reading, the middle shows how the couple travels from the shared wish to the main task: what it does and what it goes through. In tail 3-7-13 the road is travelled by chariot.

Admetus's marriage began with a harness. A lion and a boar in one chariot are animals that do not run together: one wins by pride and the leap, the other charges stubbornly straight ahead. It is a good picture of a couple with this tail: two very different temperaments yoked to one cart, pulling. Couples like this solve things by moving — a move, a renovation, a new job, a project, a sprint. Lisovskaya describes The Chariot in a couple as a team in which each grows in their own way, decisions are made together and each is quick to defend the other; what matters is to walk side by side, each on their own road.

But there is a detail that is easy to miss. It was not Admetus who yoked the beasts, it was Apollo. Wen writes that the charioteer's will comes from above: "strong positive external forces, spiritual in nature and inexplicable, have put the momentum in the Seeker." Waite adds the limit: the charioteer's conquests are "manifest or external and not within himself". All of Admetus's victories are external: a god yoked the beasts, a god tricked the Fates, Heracles defeated Death. Admetus himself never once meets his own end.

Euripides writes it in the language of a race. The father tells his son: "Shamelessly hast thou fought against thy death: thy life is but transgression of thy doom" (694–695). The Chariot outruns Death — for a while. In the minus of The Chariot, Lisovskaya names the same thing without the myth: strength is taken from those closest rather than replenished by oneself, a partner is expected to give up their own goals for someone else's, responsibility is shifted. This is Admetus's bargain, only stretched out over years. One partner's career sprint runs on the other's quiet retreat. The promise that the other's plans will get their turn "later" is repeated for ten years in a row. The shared chariot becomes a reason not to ask whose road has been put off.

The moment Death enters the house, Admetus's first act is to stop the horses. He orders the Thessalians to shave their heads and dress in black: "And ye which yoke the cars four-horsed, or steeds of single frontlet, shear with steel their manes" (428–429). The chariot goes into mourning. Couples know the feeling: when a real ending arrives, the usual speed disappears, and without it neither of them knows what to do.

Even in Homer this family is about horses. Eumelus, the son of Admetus and Alcestis, drove the best mares in the Achaean army, reared by Apollo (Iliad, II, 763–767). And in the chariot race at the funeral games for Patroclus, Athena broke his yoke and he was thrown from the chariot beside the wheel (XXIII, 391–397). The chariot and the funeral meet in the next generation too.

The strong Chariot of this tail is heard at the end of the tragedy. Admetus does not want to take into his house the woman Heracles claims to have won at the games, and Heracles answers: "Yet thy friend's victory is surely thine" (1103). In the Greek, "to win along with" is a single verb: συννικᾷς. A victory shared between two is the plus of the middle.

sections.h2: Main task — Death: the thing that cannot be outrun
paragraphs: For Lisovskaya, a couple's main task is read mostly through the minus: what is not working for the couple and what it has to learn. Among the tasks she gives Death in a couple are helping each other separate from their parents, accepting a partner utterly unlike the previous one, living through crises as a test, and seeing one's own mistakes, not only the other person's. In Alcestis each of these tasks gets its own scene.

Separating from the parents is the loudest scene in the play. Over his wife's body Admetus disowns his father and mother, and his father answers him point by point: "Thee I begat and nurtured, of mine house the heir: no debt is mine to die for thee" (681–682). The quarrel is about inheritance and debt, and that is a clue as well. Wen writes: "Traditionally, Key 13 is related to death and birth, property and inheritance, society and family, war and treaties." That is exactly what father and son are settling over the coffin: who owes whom what, and under which agreement. In Euripides the separation happens in the minus — through a curse. In the plus the task is the same, but without the trial: to separate as two, without demanding that the older generation pay for one's home, and without taking revenge for a refusal.

Other people's mistakes instead of one's own — that is the second layer of the same scene. Admetus calls his father a coward, and his father hands it back: "and dost revile thy friends who will not so — and thou the coward, thou?" (701–702). The minus of this couple's main task is not the ending itself but the ways of not noticing it: find someone to blame, speed up, buy time. When something in their shared life has run its course — a role, an agreement, a city, a ritual — the couple does not finish it, it puts on speed. The ending does not go away. One of the two pays for it: their own road slowly fades, and the union drives on on their strength.

Another clue sits in Waite's list. Among the upright meanings of Death he gives "for a man, the loss of a benefactor" (the split by gender belongs to the historical list). In Euripides, Admetus calls his dead wife exactly that: εὐεργέτις, "my benefactress" (1058, in Coleridge's translation). The main loss of this tail in the minus is the loss of the one who pulled the shared cart while the other outran his time.

The third scene is the statue. Saying goodbye, Admetus promises: "And, wrought by craftsmen's cunning hands, thy form imaged, upon a couch outstretched shall lie, falling whereon, and clasping with mine hands, calling thy name… A chill delight, I wot" (348–354). He swears there will be no more feasts in the house, no garlands, no lyre and no flute. The Empress's house freezes in mourning. Among the reversed meanings of Death, Waite lists "petrifaction". **For this couple, petrifaction means holding on to a statue of the old relationship when the living partner has already changed.** "We've always done it this way", "that's not the person I married", "let's go back to how it was in the first year" — these are conversations with a statue.

The turn in the main task is one short sentence. Back from the funeral, Admetus for the first time speaks not about his parents' cowardice but about himself: "But I, unmeet to live, my doom outrun, shall drag out bitter days: I know it now" (939–940; in Greek ἄρτι μανθάνω, "only now do I understand"). This is where the task starts to be done: when the couple stops looking for whoever should have paid, and sees its own part.

sections.h2: The Star at the centre of the couple: in Waite, "Truth unveiled"
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's chart is the atmosphere inside the union, what is not on show. In every couple with tail 3-7-13 the centre holds 17, The Star. In a personal chart, 17 never stands at the centre, for any date. So **this atmosphere exists only between two people** — neither partner brings it with them.

Lisovskaya describes The Star in the atmosphere as a union that inspires both partners. They say plainly what they like and what they don't, and often only next to each other do they understand who they want to be. It is the rare case where the pretty picture is true. The minus of the same card is things left unsaid, fitting the partner to one's own image, beautiful wrapping with nothing inside.

Waite writes that "for the majority of prepared minds, the figure will appear as the type of Truth unveiled, glorious in undying beauty." And the ending of Alcestis is built around a veil. Heracles brings in a woman wrapped from head to foot; Admetus does not recognise her and still sees something familiar: "know that thy body's stature is as Alcestis, and thy form as hers" (1062–1063). Heracles uncovers her face: "Look on her, if in aught she seems to thee like to thy wife. Step forth from grief to bliss" (1121–1122). The truth literally comes out from under its covering.

Before that, the house had it the other way round. Admetus hid his wife's death from his guest, calling the dead woman a "stranger", and Heracles feasted in a garland in a house of mourning. His first words on his return are the rule of The Star: "Unto a friend behoveth speech outspoken, Admetus, not to hide within the breast murmurs unvoiced" (1008–1010). The handsome front of a hospitable house over a hidden grief is the minus of this centre. The plus is what gets said out loud.

In Waite's list of divinatory meanings, The Star comes first as "Loss, theft, privation, abandonment", and only then "another reading says — hope and bright prospects". The play follows this list. First loss and abandonment: Admetus stands at his door knowing that inside he will see "my wife's couch tenantless, and seats whereon she sat, and, 'neath the roof, all foul the floor", and the children weeping for their mother. Then the thing nobody dared to hope for. Waite calls "hope" the summary of "several tawdry explanations". In Euripides what sounds instead is the unhoped-for: "Marvel this unhoped for!" (1123), "Past hope I have thee" (1134), and the final chorus — "Manifold things unhoped-for the Gods to accomplishment bring" (1160–1161).

Wen writes that "The Star card appears chronologically in the Major Arcana after a great deal of pain: The Hanged Man, Death, The Devil, and The Tower", and calls it a card of divine charity: "giving more than the Seeker receives". For this couple, that is the delicate point. The Star's generosity at the centre slides easily into the minus of the main task: one partner gives more than they receive, and one day gives themselves away entirely. The Star here is not a sacrifice but the truth told in time.

And one more piece of arithmetic. For a single person, the entry to the tail always equals the main task plus the centre. For this couple the rule holds only thanks to The Star: 13 + 17 = 30 → 3. Death and The Star together give The Empress. In our reading: **an ending plus the truth make a new home.**

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: a hand held out as if to the Gorgon
paragraphs: Heracles sets Admetus a condition: keep the prize woman in his house until he returns from Thrace. Admetus refuses — he has sworn that no other woman will enter his house. Heracles insists, and Admetus gives in: "I stretch it forth, as to a headless Gorgon" (1118). He holds out his hand with his face turned away, like Perseus, who looked at Medusa only in a reflection so as not to be turned to stone.

Both sides of the main task meet in this gesture. Admetus is afraid of turning to stone if he looks change in the face — but he turned to stone earlier, when he ordered himself a statue. **The strong version of 3-7-13 is to take the partner's hand even when they seem a stranger.** After a move, the birth of a child, a change of profession, a hard year, the person alongside may come back different. Lisovskaya describes the plus of Death in just these terms: the partners accept each other's past, adapt quickly to changes of mood and appearance, and keep going.

At first Admetus asks: "What if this be some phantom from the shades?" (1127). Plato's Symposium puts the difference bluntly. To Orpheus the gods showed "only a wraith of the woman for whom he came", because "he contrived the means of entering Hades alive", while Alcestis's soul was sent back because she was willing to go through death (179b–d, translated by Harold N. Fowler). A couple that tries to pass through an ending alive and untouched gets back a phantom of the old relationship. A couple that goes through the ending gets back a living person.

The gesture at the end has appeared in the play before. Remembering his wedding, Admetus says: "For with torches aflame of the Pelian pine, and with bride-song I came in that hour divine, upbearing the hand of a wife" (915–917). At the end he takes her by the hand again and leads her into the same house. The same gesture, the same person — and a different marriage.

Then comes a pause. Admetus asks why his wife is silent, and Heracles answers: "'Tis not vouchsafed thee yet to hear her voice, ere to the Powers beneath the earth she be unconsecrated, and the third day come" (1144–1146). A transition takes time. After a big change a partner may not find the old words, and to demand them at once is to call the statue back.

Admetus's last words are rendered freely in the translations. Literally they say: "now we have re-tuned our life to a better one than before" (1157–1158, literal translation). The verb μεθαρμόζω means "to rearrange, to refit in a new way". Not "we got back what we had", but "we put it together anew". This is Death in the plus: the same two people in a new arrangement. As he leaves, Heracles gives a single parting instruction: "and, just man as thou art, henceforth, Admetus, reverence still the guest" (1147–1148). The Empress's house stays hospitable, but no longer with a front over a hidden grief.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or The Devil
paragraphs: "The couple's values" is the spiritual purpose of the union, what it exists for. In couples with tail 3-7-13 two cards stand here: The Lovers in 69.1% and The Devil in 30.9%. Both answer one question the tail keeps asking: what it means to "have" another person. What follows is our reading.

The verb that runs through Alcestis is the Greek ἔχειν, "to hold, to have". Over the future statue Admetus says his arms shall "hold my belovèd, though I hold her not" (352). At the end Heracles asks: "Hast her?" — "I have" (1119), then: "all thou didst desire thou hast" (1132), and Admetus replies: "Past hope I have thee" (1134). Two ways of holding: embracing an image, and holding a living hand.

**The Lovers** as a value is a choice made freely and made again. Alcestis did not have to die; she agreed. Plato stresses that she "alone was willing". For a couple, this is the value of choosing each other again, especially after a change, the way Admetus chooses to hold out his hand to a stranger. In the minus of The Lovers, Lisovskaya names idealisation and perfectionism — the same statue, seen from the other side.

**The Devil** as a value is an honest look at attachment. Lisovskaya's conclusion about the fifteenth energy: nobody belongs to anybody. The vow that "no other wife will enter this house" and the statue in the bed are the Devil's version: holding a person as property even after the end. For a couple with The Devil in its values, one simple question helps in any change: whose decision is this, and who owes whom what?

sections.h2: What the numbers of tail 3-7-13 say
paragraphs: Tail 3-7-13 occurs in about one couple in 23 (4.28%) and ranks third of the 97 couple tails. It is a common tail that no single person ever has: in a personal chart the entry equals the main task plus the centre, and with a main task of 13 an entry of 3 would need a centre of 17, which people do not have.

It is made from only four combinations of the partners' personal tails: 15-20-5 + 15-5-8 (43% of these couples), 12-19-7 + 18-6-6 (28%), 12-16-4 + 18-9-9 (28%) and 21-10-7 + 9-15-6 (under 1%). Three clues follow from this.

**Death is in neither personal tail.** The couple's main task is always an unfolded sum of two ordinary personal tasks: 5 + 8, 6 + 7 or 4 + 9. By our count, in 42.5% of these couples neither partner has 13 at any of the main points of their chart. In working through her own example, Lisovskaya reads such an absence as an experience the couple lives through together for the first time.

**The Chariot, by contrast, is familiar to almost everyone.** In 94% of these couples at least one partner has it among the main points of their personal chart. In 43% it stands at one partner's personal centre (tail 15-5-8), and in another 29% it is one partner's personal karmic task (12-19-7 or 21-10-7). One of the two already knew how to drive before they met. Only this union teaches them how to end things. Which of the two holds the reins, the numbers do not say.

**The Chariot stands where The Tower should be.** The ends of the tail give 3 + 13 = 16 — The Tower, the collapse of the house. But a couple's middle is not worked out from the ends; it is added up from the partners' personal middles, and here that sum is always 25 → 7: 20 + 5, 19 + 6, 16 + 9 or 15 + 10. In couples with the same entry 3 and the same main task 13, the middle comes in only two kinds: The Chariot in 85.5% and The Tower in 14.5% (that is a separate tail, 3-16-13, with the same Star at the centre). And in 28% of 3-7-13 couples The Tower is there after all — in one partner's personal middle (tail 12-16-4). In the couple it adds up with the other partner's Hermit (16 + 9 = 25 → 7) and becomes The Chariot. **Where the arithmetic of the ends expects the house to fall, this couple's house does not collapse — it is driven on ahead.** That is exactly what makes the minus dangerous: a chariot makes it easy not to stop where something needs to end.
There are no other couple tails made of the numbers 3, 7 and 13: a couple's tail always begins with a multiple of three, and the order 3-13-7 does not occur in any couple.
The partners were born one day apart. First, their personal tails.

The first partner, 05.07.1975: day 5, month 7, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Karmic task 5 + 7 + 22 = 34 → 7. Centre 5 + 7 + 22 + 7 = 41 → 5. The entry to the tail is the task plus the centre: 7 + 5 = 12; the middle is the task plus the entry: 7 + 12 = 19. Personal tail 12-19-7.
The second partner, 04.07.1975: day 4, month 7, year 22. Task 4 + 7 + 22 = 33 → 6, centre 4 + 7 + 22 + 6 = 39 → 12, entry 6 + 12 = 18, middle 6 + 18 = 24 → 6. Personal tail 18-6-6.
Now each point of the couple is added up from the partners' points of the same name:
The middle is 19 + 6, not 3 + 13: the sum of the ends is not used here. These two people's "couple's values" are 6, The Lovers.

The example shows the clues from the section on numbers well. Both partners have The Chariot at the month point — both were born in July. For the first it is also the personal karmic task; for the second it appears four times in the chart. And 13 and 17 are absent from every main point of both charts: Death and The Star are an experience that appears for them only together. In this couple's chart both cards repeat: Death also stands at "What connects", and The Star at "Path to prosperity". Lisovskaya draws attention to repeats like these: an energy that stands at several points sounds louder in the couple.

sections.h2: How a couple can live tail 3-7-13
paragraphs: The task of the tail is not to want less and drive slower. The Empress and The Chariot are strong cards; without them the couple would have neither a home nor momentum. The task is to learn the third thing.

ol: **Name endings out loud.** When something in shared life has run its course — a role, an agreement, a city, a ritual — say "this is over" before reaching for the accelerator.
**Check who is paying for the race.** Every so often ask: whose road have we put off for the sake of the shared chariot? If the answer is always the same person, that is Admetus's bargain.
**Don't talk to the statue.** "That's not the person I married" is not an argument. Comparing a partner with who they were is embracing a cold image.
**Give a change three days.** After a big change, don't demand the old words at once: silence is part of the transition, not a refusal.
**Speak freely to a friend.** Heracles' rule: a reproach kept in silence does more harm than one spoken. A home does not have to look happy for the guests.
**Separate from the parents as two.** Don't build the shared home on the older generation paying for it with money, time or themselves, and don't condemn them for refusing.
**Hold out a hand even when it is frightening.** After a change a partner may seem a stranger. That is no reason to turn away for good — it is a reason to look.

intro: Death in the destiny matrix does not foretell events. It is the card of a change of form: an old way of living, a role or an agreement comes to an end so that the union can go on in a new shape. The couple's karmic tail 3-7-13 reads like this:

ul: **3 · The Empress — entry to the task.** What the couple wants together: a home where there is plenty of everything, guests, children, plans — and for it all to last. The couple enters its task through this wish, and later runs up against it.
**7 · The Chariot — middle of the task.** How the couple travels the road: in one harness, at speed, through victories. Two very different characters pull one cart.

**13 · Death — main task.** Letting go of what has run its course, and not handing the change over to the other person. In the minus it becomes a race in which the couple outruns every ending, and one of the two pays for it.

intro: The story was written down almost two and a half thousand years ago. The myth of Admetus and Alcestis, which Euripides turned into his tragedy Alcestis, has all of it: a house famous for its plenty, a chariot drawn by a lion and a boar, and Death, who comes for the king's wife in person. What follows is an investigation: what is written into the three cards, into the books of Waite, Wen and Lisovskaya, and into numbers checked against every possible date.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 3-7-13 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of the couple's chart: The Empress at the entry, The Chariot in the middle, Death as the main task. The couple wants a full home and growth, goes after it through motion and victories, and has to learn to end the outworn forms of the union and accept each other changed. It occurs in about one couple in 23.

faq.q: Does Death in a couple's tail predict a break-up or disaster?
faq.a: No. The numbers of the chart do not predict events, dates or outcomes. Death in the destiny matrix is the card of a change of form: a way of living, a role or an agreement ends, and the union continues in a new shape. If someone in a couple is seriously afraid for their safety, that is not a question for the cards: call a local emergency number or a crisis line and talk to a psychologist.

faq.q: Why does tail 3-7-13 occur only in a couple's chart?
faq.a: In a personal chart, the entry to the tail equals the main task plus the centre. With a main task of 13, an entry of 3 would need a centre of 17, and no person has that centre. In a couple, the centre 17, The Star, appears in every case with this tail, which is why it adds up — but only for two people.

They share the same ends and the same Star at the centre, but the middle differs. In 3-7-13 the road runs through The Chariot — motion, a sprint, a shared harness. In 3-16-13 it runs through The Tower, the collapse of what was. Tail 3-16-13 is much rarer, found in about 0.7% of couples.

faq.q: In a couple with tail 3-7-13, who is Admetus and who is Alcestis?
faq.a: The tail does not divide roles by gender and does not name a culprit. Either partner can be the "Admetus" who outruns his endings or the "Alcestis" who pays for the shared race with herself, and often the two take turns. The tail describes what happens between two people, not the character of one.

report: King Admetus won his bride with a chariot that a god had yoked to a lion and a boar — and later let her die in his place. Euripides turned this myth into his tragedy Alcestis, and its three acts run exactly in the order of the cards of tail 3-7-13: a house with plenty of everything — The Empress; a chariot drawn by two animals that do not belong together — The Chariot; and Death, who in Euripides walks in at the door in person. **A couple with this tail can outrun almost anything. What it has to learn is the one thing nobody outruns: how to end a form that has run its course and meet the partner again, as someone new.**

Death here is neither an event nor a verdict but the card of a change of form: a way of living, a role or an agreement ends so that the union can go on in a new shape. In the myth Admetus is the husband and Alcestis the wife, but in a couple gender does not hand out the roles. Either partner can be the "Admetus" who outruns his own endings, and either can be the "Alcestis" who pays for the shared race with herself. Often the two take turns.

report.h3: A home with plenty of everything, for good

report: At the entry stands The Empress — the couple's shared wish, its "common language". That language sounds like "more, and for good": a bigger flat, a long table for friends and family, children, a business that keeps growing. People like this are warm to be around, and it is not an act. Admetus's house in Euripides is the model: even on the day of the funeral the host will not turn a guest away, because "mine halls have not learnt to thrust away nor to dishonour guests".

The minus is hidden in the vocabulary. In Waite's list of divinatory meanings, The Empress has "length of days". In Coleridge's English translation, these are the very words Admetus throws at his father, and the father accuses him of the same: both want a long life. **In the minus, the wish at the entry sounds like this: let it all be ours, and let nothing ever end.** Admetus expected his parents to pay for his life, and took offence when they refused: "For in word only, not in deed, they loved me." In an ordinary couple it is quieter: the plan for the big home rests on the parents' money, on somebody's unpaid work, on one of the two agreeing to "wait for now".

report.h3: A lion and a boar in one harness

report: In the middle of the tail stands The Chariot: this is how the couple travels its road. Two very different temperaments are yoked to one cart, pulling. Couples like this solve things by moving — a move, a renovation, a new job, a sprint — and in the plus they are a team that decides together and is quick to defend each other.

But it was Apollo who yoked the beasts for Admetus, not Admetus himself. Waite writes that the charioteer's conquests are "manifest or external and not within himself". All of Admetus's victories are external: a god yoked the beasts, a god tricked the Fates, Heracles defeated Death. His father tells him: "thy life is but transgression of thy doom". The Chariot outruns Death — for a while, and someone else pays for it. Lisovskaya describes the same minus without the myth: strength is taken from those closest rather than replenished by oneself, and a partner is expected to give up their own goals. One partner's career sprint runs on the other's quiet retreat, and the promise that the other's plans will get their turn "later" is repeated for ten years in a row.

Euripides gives the plus of the middle to Heracles: "Yet thy friend's victory is surely thine." In the Greek, "to win along with" is a single verb. A victory shared between two, not borrowed from one of them.

The main task is Death, and it is read through the minus: not the ending itself but the ways of not noticing it. Find someone to blame, speed up, buy time. Over his wife's body Admetus calls his father a coward, and his father hands it back: "and dost revile thy friends who will not so — and thou the coward, thou?"

Saying goodbye to Alcestis, Admetus promises to have craftsmen make her statue, to take it to bed and call it by her name: "A chill delight, I wot." There will be no more feasts in the house, no garlands, no music — The Empress's house freezes in mourning. Among the reversed meanings of Death, Waite lists "petrifaction". **For this couple, petrifaction means holding on to a statue of the old relationship when the living partner has already changed.** "We've always done it this way", "that's not the person I married" — these are conversations with a statue.

The turn is a single sentence. Back from the funeral, Admetus for the first time speaks about himself rather than his parents' cowardice, and ends with the words "I know it now". This is where the task starts to be done: when the couple stops looking for whoever should have paid, and sees its own part.

report.h3: A hand held out as if to the Gorgon

report: Heracles brings a veiled woman into the house and insists that Admetus take her hand. Admetus obeys with his face turned away: "I stretch it forth, as to a headless Gorgon." He is afraid of turning to stone if he looks change in the face — but he turned to stone earlier, when he ordered himself a statue. Heracles uncovers her face: "Look on her." It is Alcestis. **The strong version of the tail is to take the partner's hand even when they seem a stranger:** after a move, the birth of a child, a change of profession, a hard year.

This is where the couple's centre does its work — The Star, an atmosphere that arises only between two people. Waite writes that the figure of The Star appears as "the type of Truth unveiled". Before the ending, the house had it the other way round: Admetus hid his wife's death from his guest, and a handsome front stood over a hidden grief. Heracles' first words are the rule of The Star: speak freely to a friend, and do not keep reproaches in silence.

For three days Alcestis is silent: a transition takes time, and to demand the old words at once is to call the statue back. Literally, Admetus's last words say: "now we have re-tuned our life to a better one than before". Not "we got back what we had", but "we put it together anew". The first time, he led his wife into the house by the hand to the sound of wedding songs; at the end he leads her in again — the same gesture, the same person, and a different marriage. **Death in the plus is the same two people in a new arrangement.**

unit.title: A hand held out to the Gorgon

captions.M: To want a full house — more, and for good
captions.N: To race in one harness and win together
captions.D: To end what has run its course and accept a changed partner

unit.meaning: Your task is not to outrun change but to end the outworn together and take the hand of a partner who has come back changed.
